title: The Sleeping Visitor
premise: Kestrel Sandoval, an obsessive urban explorer who documents everything as a form of prayer, maps tunnels beneath the drowned town of Vesper Hollow that appear on no survey. His sleep recordings begin capturing a second voice — dry, patient, answering questions he never asked aloud — and he realizes the tunnels are dreaming him back toward 1974, when the town's last resident, Alma Reyes, was made to sign away something that was never hers to give. As the voice wears his own memories like a borrowed coat, Kestrel must return what was taken — Alma's name, written into the deed of a thing that sleeps below — before the county's final paperwork erases Vesper Hollow and its resident forever. He succeeds only by surrendering his own documentation, his prayer, his proof that he existed, and walks out of the tunnels a man no record can confirm.
about_author: Theo Joubert is the pen name of a former municipal archivist who spent eleven years cataloguing condemned properties in the American Southwest before leaving to write full-time. He lives near a reservoir and has never learned to swim.

chapters.title: Everything Is a Prayer
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. We meet him documenting the Vesper Hollow reservoir ruins, his rituals of notation, and his discovery that his laser-surveyed tunnels match no county record. Emotional beat: the thrill of being the only one who knows — the first flush of power that will corrupt him.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Reviewing sleep recordings to track his own sleepwalking, he hears a dry, patient voice answering questions he never asked. He cross-references dates with tunnel collapses in 1974. Emotional beat: dread braided with fascination — he starts talking back in his sleep on purpose.

chapters.title: Deed of the Drowned
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Alma Reyes, 94, in a care facility, resisting her grandson's push to sign final county dissolution papers for Vesper Hollow. She keeps saying the town was never sold, only lent. Emotional beat: her stubborn, frightened dignity; Kestrel finds her through the 1974 documents.

chapters.title: What the Tunnels Remember
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, deepening descent. He maps a chamber where the walls are covered in handwriting — his own handwriting, dated 1974. The voice explains, gently, that documentation is a door, and his notebooks have been knocking for years. Emotional beat: identity begins to slip; he can't prove which memories are his.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Coat
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. He wakes wearing clothes that fit him wrong, with mud from a tunnel that was flooded in '74. The voice has started using his mother's phrases, his dead brother's laugh. Alma calls him — she dreamed his face. Emotional beat: terror of being overwritten by something that loves him incorrectly.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: Alma's POV, a full chapter inside her memory of the signing: the men from the water authority, the document that transferred not land but her name into the town's deed, binding the sleeping thing below to obey whoever holds it. Emotional beat: grief and rage; the reader learns what 'returning' actually requires.

chapters.title: The Grandson's Papers
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Alma's grandson, needing the signature for money, arrives at the ruins with the dissolution papers, and Kestrel realizes the county's paperwork is the same ritual as 1974 — power repeating itself. The voice offers Kestrel the deed instead: hold the town, hold the power. Emotional beat: temptation at its most reasonable.

chapters.title: Sign Here
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, climax begins. He takes the offered deed and feels the tunnels rearrange around his will — roads unbending, water receding — and understands within hours what it costs: the thing below feeds on recorded memory, and he is the richest archive it has ever held. Emotional beat: the corruption theme made flesh; power feels exactly like being loved.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Climax. Kestrel, half-erased, carries the original 1974 deed to the chamber and convinces Alma — brought down in her wheelchair by the grandson's guilt — to speak her own name back into it. The voice screams in Kestrel's mother's voice. He burns his notebooks, his recordings, his proof. Emotional beat: sacrifice as the only honest prayer.

chapters.title: No Record of Him
chapters.summary: Alma's POV, then a coda in county records. The dissolution papers are signed; Vesper Hollow passes as ordinary drowned land. Alma remembers a young man who walked her out of the tunnels and no one else does. Kestrel surfaces, undocumented, free, and chooses not to write any of it down. Emotional beat: quiet, hard-won peace — identity kept by memory alone.
